title: Quantum Computers Aren't Faster Computers
dek: They don't try every answer at once. They do something stranger, it only pays off on a short list of problems, and one of those problems happens to be the lock on the internet.

blocks.text: In December 2024, Google announced a chip called Willow. It finished a benchmark calculation in under five minutes. Google estimated that one of the fastest classical supercomputers on Earth would need about 10 septillion years to do the same job. That's a 1 followed by 25 zeros, far longer than the universe has existed.

Read that and it's natural to imagine your next gaming PC running on qubits, loading instantly, rendering at a million frames per second. It won't. Willow can't run a web browser, and the problem it crushed was chosen because it is brutally hard for normal computers and almost useless for anything else.

So here's the puzzle: how can a machine be septillions of times faster than a supercomputer at one task and worse than your phone at almost everything else? The answer is the single most misunderstood idea in modern technology. A quantum computer isn't a faster computer. It's a different kind of instrument, and once you understand how it really works, you can tell the hype from the genuinely big deal.
The myth of trying every answer at once

Start with what a normal computer does. A *bit* is a switch that's either 0 or 1. Your CPU flips billions of them per second in a precise sequence. At every moment, the machine is in exactly one definite state, and you could, in principle, read out every bit without disturbing anything.

A *qubit* is different. Its state is described by two numbers called *amplitudes*, one attached to 0 and one attached to 1. Amplitudes behave a lot like waves: they have a size and a direction, so they can be positive, negative, or something in between. When you measure the qubit, you get a plain 0 or a plain 1, with odds set by the squared size of each amplitude. The measurement also destroys the delicate in-between state.

Now add more qubits. Two qubits need four amplitudes, one for each combination: 00, 01, 10, 11. Three need eight. Every added qubit doubles the count, so 300 qubits involve 2 to the 300th power amplitudes, a number vastly larger than the count of atoms in the observable universe. This is where the popular story comes from: a quantum computer explores all those possibilities in parallel, so it must be checking every answer at once.

Those combined amplitudes are also where *entanglement* comes from. When qubits are entangled, the amplitudes can't be split into separate descriptions for each qubit. The system only makes sense as a whole: measure one qubit and you instantly constrain what the others can show. Entanglement isn't a way to send messages faster than light, but it is the resource that lets a computation weave the possibilities of many qubits together instead of treating each one alone.

Here's the catch that the popular story leaves out. When you measure at the end, you get one answer, chosen at random according to the amplitudes. If all the possible answers have equal amplitudes, you just get a random guess. You could do that with a coin. All that enormous hidden state is worthless unless you can arrange for the wrong answers to fade and the right one to stand out before you look.

A quantum computer doesn't check every answer and report back. It sets up a pattern of waves so that wrong answers cancel each other out, then takes one measurement and hopes the right answer is the loudest thing left.
Interference is the real trick

If you've worked with AC power, you already have the intuition. Two signals in phase add up. Two signals 180 degrees out of phase cancel. Noise-cancelling headphones use the same idea, generating a wave that is the mirror image of the noise so that the two sum to nearly nothing.

Quantum algorithms are choreography for that kind of cancellation. Each step of the computation is a *gate*, an operation that rotates and mixes the amplitudes. A well-designed sequence of gates makes the paths leading to wrong answers arrive out of phase, so they cancel, while the paths leading to the right answer arrive in phase and reinforce. Then you measure, and with high probability you get the answer you wanted.

The hard part is that you can only build this choreography when the problem has some hidden structure the waves can lock onto, like a repeating pattern. Most everyday computing tasks have no such structure to exploit. That's why there is no quantum spreadsheet and probably never will be. The speedup is not a general property of the hardware. It belongs to specific algorithms for specific problems.

blocks.title: How a quantum algorithm actually runs
items: Prepare the qubits in a simple starting state, usually all zeros.
Apply gates that spread the amplitudes across many possible answers.
Apply more gates that encode the problem, shifting the phase of some paths.
Use interference so wrong answers cancel and the right one grows.
Measure once and read out a single classical answer.
Repeat several times and check the result on a normal computer.

blocks.text: The short list of things it's good at

The most famous example came in 1994, when Peter Shor, then at AT&T, showed that a quantum computer could factor large numbers efficiently. Factoring means taking a number like 15 and finding the primes that multiply to make it, 3 and 5. For numbers hundreds of digits long, the best known classical methods take an impractically long time. Shor's algorithm turns factoring into a problem of finding the period of a repeating pattern, exactly the kind of structure that interference can latch onto.

In 1996, Lov Grover at Bell Labs found a broader but much smaller speedup. Imagine a phone directory of N names in random order, and you want the one with a given number. A classical search has to check about half the entries on average. Grover's algorithm needs only about the square root of N steps. For a million entries, that's on the order of a thousand steps instead of half a million. Useful, but it's a square-root gain, not the exponential leap Shor offers.

The third big category may matter most in the long run: simulating nature itself. Molecules and materials are quantum systems, and tracking their electrons on a classical computer gets exponentially harder as they grow. A quantum computer speaks the same language as the thing it's simulating. That's the hope behind designing better catalysts, batteries and drugs, and it's the area Google pointed to in October 2025 with an algorithm called Quantum Echoes, aimed at revealing hidden dynamics inside quantum systems like molecules.

blocks.title: Where quantum helps, and where it doesn't

left.head: Strong candidates
items: Factoring big numbers (Shor)
Simulating molecules and materials
Some search and optimization problems, with smaller gains
Sampling tasks designed to be hard classically

right.head: Poor fits
items: Gaming, video and graphics
Web browsing and everyday apps
Most business software and databases
Anything that needs to read out huge amounts of data

blocks.text: The noise problem

If quantum computing is so powerful for these problems, why haven't we broken anything yet? Because qubits are absurdly fragile. Any stray interaction with the outside world, whether heat, vibration or a passing electromagnetic field, leaks information out of the qubit and scrambles the amplitudes. Physicists call this *decoherence*. Superconducting chips like Google's are cooled to a tiny fraction of a degree above absolute zero to slow it down, and even so, Willow's qubits hold their state for times approaching 100 microseconds.

Every gate also has a small chance of error. Google reported fidelities for Willow of 99.97 percent for single-qubit gates and 99.88 percent for the two-qubit gates that create entanglement. That sounds excellent until you remember that a useful algorithm needs millions or billions of operations, and errors stack up.

items.label: Physical qubits on Google's Willow chip
How long Willow's qubits hold their state
Fidelity of Willow's two-qubit gates

blocks.source: Google Quantum AI, Willow announcement (Dec 2024) and hardware update (Oct 2025)

blocks.text: The answer is *quantum error correction*. You spread one reliable *logical* qubit across many unreliable *physical* qubits and keep checking them for signs of damage, without directly measuring the information you're protecting. It's a bit like a RAID array or redundant instrument channels in a reactor plant: no single sensor is trusted, but the group can catch and correct a failure. The catch is that more qubits also means more places for errors to creep in. Error correction only wins if the hardware is already good enough. That cutoff is called the *threshold*.

There's a clever twist in how the checking works. You can't just look at the protected qubits, because measuring them would destroy the information. Instead, extra helper qubits are entangled with groups of data qubits and measured in their place. Their results reveal whether a neighbor has flipped, without revealing what the data actually is. A classical computer reads those results continuously and decides which corrections to apply, over and over in a continuous cycle for as long as the computation runs.

Willow's real headline wasn't the septillion years. It was that when Google grew its encoded qubit from a 3-by-3 grid of physical qubits to 5-by-5 and then 7-by-7, the error rate fell by half at each step. Bigger finally meant better. That's the first convincing sign that scaling up can work, though a useful machine needs vastly more qubits than 105.
A countdown on the internet's lock

Much of the internet's security has relied on public-key cryptography such as RSA, which depends on factoring being hopelessly slow. A big enough quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would break it. So the question that matters is not whether a quantum computer is impressive. It's how big one would need to be.

In 2019, Craig Gidney and Martin Ekerå estimated that factoring a 2048-bit RSA key would take about 20 million noisy physical qubits running for eight hours. In May 2025, Gidney published a new estimate: fewer than a million noisy qubits, running for less than a week, assuming the same error rate of 0.1 percent per gate. The hardware didn't get 20 times better in six years. The *algorithms* did. That's a pattern worth remembering: in this field, the target moves from both ends.

blocks.title: Qubits needed to break RSA-2048 vs. qubits built
blocks.note: The 2025 figure is an upper bound ('less than a million'). Willow's bar is there; at 105 qubits it's too small to see.
blocks.source: Gidney & Ekerå, 2019; Gidney, arXiv 2505.15917, 2025; Google Quantum AI, 2024

blocks.text: Even so, the gap is enormous. Today's best chips have around a hundred physical qubits, and the requirement is still on the order of a million. Nobody can tell you with confidence when that gap closes. But there's a reason security agencies are moving now. Adversaries can record encrypted traffic today and simply store it, waiting for the day they can decrypt it. Security people call this *harvest now, decrypt later*. Secrets that need to stay secret for decades are already exposed to a future machine.

That's why, in August 2024, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalized its first three post-quantum encryption standards, built on math problems that are believed to be hard for quantum computers too. One is meant for general encryption and two for digital signatures. NIST noted that some experts expect a code-breaking quantum computer within a decade. The software migration is starting long before the hardware exists, which is exactly how it should work.

blocks.title: From theory to countdown
items: Peter Shor shows a quantum computer could factor large numbers efficiently
Lov Grover publishes a square-root speedup for unstructured search
Google's 53-qubit Sycamore claims a task in 200 seconds; IBM counters that a supercomputer could do it in about 2.5 days

NIST finalizes its first three post-quantum encryption standards

blocks.text: How to read the next headline

The 2019 Sycamore claim is a useful lesson. Google said its 53-qubit chip did in 200 seconds what a supercomputer would need 10,000 years to do. IBM quickly argued that a smarter classical approach on the Summit supercomputer could do it in about 2.5 days. Classical algorithms keep improving too, so every claim of quantum advantage is a race against a moving target. Some claims hold up, and some shrink.

It also helps to know what the famous benchmark actually is. *Random circuit sampling* means running a random jumble of gates and collecting the outputs. The results have no practical meaning. The point is that the pattern of outputs is extraordinarily hard to reproduce on a classical machine, which makes it a good stress test and a poor product. Google's October 2025 Quantum Echoes work was pitched as a step past this, because its result can be checked and is connected to real physics questions about molecules.

When you see the next big announcement, ask three questions. Is the task useful, or was it chosen because it's hard for classical machines? Can the answer be checked? And how many of the qubits are error-corrected logical qubits rather than raw physical ones? Those three questions cut through most of the noise.

The reframe to carry around is this. A quantum computer is to a normal computer what a telescope is to a truck. Nobody asks whether a telescope is faster than a truck. It does something a truck can't do at all, and it's useless for hauling groceries. The machines being built now are early, noisy telescopes. What they eventually reveal, whether it's new materials, new medicines or the contents of today's encrypted messages, depends on how fast the engineering closes a gap that is still measured in factors of ten thousand.

takeaways: Qubits hold many amplitudes, but a measurement gives one answer. The power comes from interference, not from checking every answer.
Big speedups exist only for problems with hidden structure: factoring, simulating molecules, and a few others.
Noise is the main obstacle; error correction spreads one logical qubit across many physical ones and only works below a quality threshold.
Breaking RSA-2048 was estimated at 20 million qubits in 2019 and under a million in 2025. Today's best chips have about a hundred.
Post-quantum encryption standards were finalized in 2024 because encrypted data can be stored now and decrypted later.

title: The Feed Knows What You'll Do, Not What You Want
dek: Recommendation algorithms are prediction machines aimed at your behavior. Once you see how they score you, the endless scroll stops looking like a window and starts looking like a mirror.

blocks.text: It's 0130 and you just got off watch. You tell yourself you'll check one thing before you rack out. Forty minutes later you're watching a stranger restore a rusted pocketknife, and you couldn't explain how you got there if someone paid you. You didn't really choose most of those videos. You just never said no to them.

That isn't a character flaw so much as an engineering result. In January 2018, YouTube's chief product officer, Neal Mohan, said that about 70 percent of the time people spend watching YouTube is driven by its recommendations. Netflix engineers wrote in 2015 that their recommender influenced roughly 80 percent of the hours streamed on the service. Most of what the world watches is no longer picked by the viewer. It's picked by a prediction.

To use these systems instead of being used by them, it helps to know what they actually are. They aren't mind readers, and they aren't villains. They are machines built to answer one narrow question, billions of times a day: *what will this person do next?*

items.label: Share of YouTube watch time driven by recommendations (2018)
Share of Netflix hours streamed influenced by its recommender (2015)
How long a typical Netflix member browses before losing interest

blocks.source: Neal Mohan at CES, reported by Quartz, 2018; Gomez-Uribe & Hunt, ACM Transactions on Management Information Systems, 2015

blocks.text: A funnel, not a mind

Look at the problem from the platform's side. YouTube has an enormous library and a fraction of a second to fill your home screen. No model can carefully evaluate every video for every user in that time. So almost every large recommender is built as a funnel, with cheap, fast filtering at the top and slow, careful judgment at the bottom.

Google engineers described YouTube's version in a 2016 paper. The first stage, *candidate generation*, takes a corpus of millions of videos and pulls out a few hundred that are roughly relevant to you. It leans heavily on *collaborative filtering*: the idea that people who watched what you watched tend to want what those people watched next. The second stage, *ranking*, scores each of those few hundred carefully, using many more signals. A few dozen make it to your screen.

The trick that makes the first stage fast is called an *embedding*. Every video and every user gets turned into a list of numbers, a few hundred long, which you can picture as a point in a space with hundreds of dimensions. During training, the system nudges those points around so that the things you'd watch end up close to you. Finding candidates then becomes a geometry problem: grab the videos nearest your point.

Nobody writes down that one axis means tactical gear and another means sad piano covers. The model invents its own axes from billions of clicks, and many of them don't map onto any human category at all. That's part of why a feed can feel uncannily accurate and impossible to explain at the same time.

blocks.title: How a feed gets built in a fraction of a second
items: Start with the whole library: millions of items.
Candidate generation: cheaply pull a few hundred items that sit near your embedding.
Ranking: score each candidate with a bigger model and many more signals.
Filter and mix: drop repeats, spam and things you've seen; add some variety.
Show the top results and log everything you do with them.
Feed that log back into training, so tomorrow's model knows you a little differently.

blocks.text: What the machine is really predicting

Here is the part most people miss. The ranking model doesn't output a single verdict on how good a video is. It predicts a set of separate probabilities: the chance you'll click, watch to the end, like, reply, share, or tell it to go away. Then a plain formula combines those predictions into one score, and the highest scores win. The predictions are learned from data. The formula is chosen by people, and it encodes what the company has decided to value.

YouTube's 2016 paper is unusually frank about this. Its ranking objective was described as mostly a function of expected watch time per impression, rather than the chance of a click. The reason was practical: ranking by clicks tends to promote deceptive videos that people open and then abandon. Watch time was harder to fake. Notice what happened there. A human looked at a number, saw it being gamed, and swapped it for a different number.

We rarely get to see that formula. In 2023, Twitter (now X) published code for its home timeline ranker, including the weights it used as of April 2023. Each weight multiplies the predicted probability of one action. They're worth a close look, because they turn an abstract idea into a price list.

blocks.title: Twitter's ranking weights, April 2023 (like = 0.5)
blocks.note: Negative signals were weighted too: 'show less' or block at −74, a report at −369.
blocks.source: Twitter, the-algorithm-ml, home timeline ranker README, 2023

blocks.text: Read it like a menu. On that ranking, a predicted reply was worth 27 likes. A reply that the original poster then answered was worth 150 likes. A predicted report cost as much as 738 likes. Whoever set those numbers decided that conversation matters far more than quiet approval, and they were right that conversation keeps people on the app. What the formula didn't ask was whether the conversation was a friendly one or a shouting match.

Every platform makes a version of that choice. YouTube made a famous one in March 2012, when it told creators it would weight time watched more heavily than clicks when picking related and recommended videos. Clicks had been rewarding misleading thumbnails and titles. Watch time was supposed to reward videos people actually wanted to see.
Better serve videos that keep viewers entertained.

TikTok said in 2020 that one of its strongest signals is whether you finish a longer video from beginning to end, and that follower count is not a direct factor. Each of these is a sensible proxy for 'this person liked it.' None of them is the same thing as 'this person is glad they spent the time.'
The explore-exploit trap

A recommender faces a dilemma borrowed from casinos. Computer scientists call it the *multi-armed bandit* problem. A gambler facing a row of slot machines has to choose between pulling the one that has paid well so far (exploiting) and trying others that might pay better (exploring). Exploit too much and the feed goes stale. Explore too much and it fills with junk.

So feeds do both. Most of what you see is a confident bet, and a slice of it is a probe: something slightly outside your usual range, placed there to measure your reaction. That's why a strange video sometimes appears out of nowhere, and why one long look at it can tilt your feed for days. The system isn't messing with you. It's running an experiment, and you just answered it.

There's also a bias toward the past built into any model trained on yesterday's data. The YouTube engineers found that their system, left alone, underrated brand-new uploads, because popularity in the training data was averaged over the whole training window. Their fix was to tell the model how old each training example was, which raised watch time on fresh videos. Small design choices like that decide which creators get a shot and which never surface.

Put those pieces together and you get a loop, and loops are where the interesting behavior lives. Your actions train the model. The model decides what you see. What you see shapes your next actions. Anyone who has studied control systems knows that feedback can stabilize or it can drift. Watch three videos on a topic out of pure boredom, and the system may conclude that topic is who you are.

blocks.title: The feed loop
items: You act: watch, skip, like, linger
The model updates its picture of you
The feed shifts toward that picture
Your options narrow to what it shows
You act on those options

blocks.text: The same loop runs on the people making content. Anyone building a YouTube channel or a Roblox game is optimizing against a ranking formula whether they mean to or not. Strong hooks in the first seconds, faces in thumbnails, titles that open a question: creators drift toward these because the ranker rewards whatever predicts watching. The algorithm doesn't just learn its audience. It quietly trains everyone who makes things for it.
Wanting versus liking

If these models are so good at predicting behavior, why does an hour of scrolling so often feel like an hour you'd like back? Because behavior and satisfaction are different signals, and engagement only measures one of them.

A team led by Smitha Milli tested this directly. In February 2023 they recruited 806 Twitter users and compared the tweets the engagement-based algorithm showed each person with what a plain newest-first timeline would have shown. Participants then rated the tweets. The algorithmic feed carried noticeably more anger. Anger expressed by tweet authors was about half a standard deviation higher, and readers reported feeling angrier too. (A standard deviation is a measure of how spread out a set of scores is; half of one is a moderate effect, easily big enough to change the mood of a feed.) For political tweets the gap was even larger.

Here's the part that should stick. Users said they did not prefer the political tweets the algorithm picked for them. The system was serving content people engaged with but wouldn't have chosen. That isn't a conspiracy. Anger is engaging. It makes people reply, and on that 2023 price list a reply was worth 27 likes. The algorithm did exactly what it was told.

Economists have names for the gap. *Revealed preferences* are what your behavior shows you want. *Stated preferences* are what you say you want when someone asks you calmly. Feeds are built almost entirely on the first kind, because it's abundant, automatic and cheap to collect. The second kind takes asking, and asking is slow.

There's an old warning in economics, usually credited to Charles Goodhart: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Watch time and replies started out as decent clues that people were enjoying themselves. Turn them into the thing a billion-dollar system maximizes, and the system will find every way to raise the number, including ways that have nothing to do with enjoyment.

blocks.title: Two versions of you

left.head: What the model can see
items: You watched 90 percent of it
You replied within seconds
You stopped scrolling for eight seconds
You came back an hour later

right.head: What it can't see
items: You were annoyed the whole time
You were arguing, not enjoying
You were half asleep
You wish you'd gone to bed

blocks.text: It's worth being fair, too. Recommenders solve a real problem. Netflix's own research found that a typical member loses interest after 60 to 90 seconds of browsing, having looked at maybe 10 to 20 titles. Without a recommender, most of a giant library would be invisible, and plenty of great small creators would never be found. The issue isn't recommendation itself. It's what the system is told to maximize.
A feed is a mirror that reflects what you do, never what you meant. If you want it to show you something different, the only language it understands is behavior.
Taking back the controls

Once you see the machine as a behavior predictor wrapped in a weighting formula, the defensive moves become obvious. The model can't hear your intentions. It can only count your actions. So make your actions say what you mean.

items: Don't hate-watch. Lingering on rage bait is a vote for more of it, even if you never tap anything.
Use the negative buttons. 'Not interested' and 'don't recommend this channel' exist, and the published Twitter weights show how heavily negative feedback can count.
Search on purpose. A deliberate search hands the model a clear signal about what you want.
Finish what you value and bail fast on what you don't. Completion is one of the strongest signals platforms use.
Lean on subscription or following feeds when you can; they sit closer to your stated preferences.
Prune or pause your watch history if a binge has skewed things.

blocks.text: There's one more lever, and most people never get it: real time away. Months underway with no connection means you come back to apps running on an old picture of you. The first sessions back in port are fresh evidence. Spend them deliberately, and you're giving the model a new first draft instead of letting your most bored hours write it.

The deeper reframe is this. A feed isn't showing you what you like. It's showing you what a model predicted you would do, weighted by what a company decided to count. Once you see that, the scroll stops looking like a window onto the world. It's a very good guess about you, assembled as easily from your worst five minutes as from your best.

takeaways: Recommenders predict your actions, then rank by a formula that people chose. The formula defines what 'good' means.
On Twitter's published 2023 weights, a reply was worth 27 likes, which is one reason arguments travel so well.
Engagement measures what you do, not whether you're glad you did it.
Every linger, rewatch and reply is training data; deliberate searches and 'not interested' clicks are strong signals too.
Coming back online after time away is a chance to retrain your feed on purpose.

title: Evolution on Fast Forward
dek: Antibiotics are one of the greatest inventions in history, and bacteria have been dismantling them since the first patient was treated. Watching how they do it is the clearest look at evolution you will ever get.

blocks.text: At Harvard Medical School in 2016, a team built the biggest petri dish most biologists had ever seen: a rectangle of agar two feet by four feet, about 14 liters of bacterial food. They divided it into bands. The outer edges had no drug at all. The next band held just enough of the antibiotic trimethoprim to kill ordinary *E. coli*. Each band toward the center held ten times more than the one before, until the middle strip held a thousand times the lethal dose.

Then they put bacteria on the edges, pointed a camera at the dish, and let it run. The bacteria filled the drug-free zone and stopped at the first wall of antibiotic, a wall that should have been fatal. For a while nothing happened. Then a small tuft appeared on the other side of the line: a mutant that could survive. It spread across the band and stopped at the next wall. Then another mutant broke through, and another.

Within about ten days, bacteria were growing in the center of the plate, in a thousand times the dose that had killed their ancestors. When the team tried another antibiotic, ciprofloxacin, the bacteria evolved resistance to a hundred thousand times the starting dose. The time-lapse video is one of the most striking things in modern biology, because it shows evolution happening the way it actually works: not as a slow slide but as a series of breakthroughs, each built on the last.

items.label: Trimethoprim dose E. coli survived after evolving on the MEGA-plate
Time to evolve that level of resistance
Resistance evolved against the starting dose of ciprofloxacin

blocks.source: Baym et al., Science, 2016 (Harvard Gazette)

blocks.text: Why bacteria win the arms race

Resistance is not something bacteria decide to develop, and they do not get stronger by being exposed to antibiotics the way a muscle gets stronger from training. It is natural selection, the same process Darwin described, running on a population so large and so fast that you can see it happen in a week.

Here is the math that makes it work. Under good conditions, some bacteria can divide every 20 to 30 minutes. A single infection can contain billions of cells. Every time a cell copies its DNA there is a small chance of a mistake, a mutation. Almost all mutations are useless or harmful. But when you have billions of cells dividing many times a day, even a one-in-a-billion mutation is likely to show up somewhere. If one of those happens to block the antibiotic, that cell survives while its neighbors die, and its offspring inherit the trick.

Put that in human terms. A bacterium that divides every 20 minutes can pass through about 70 generations in a single day. Seventy human generations, at roughly 25 years each, stretches back well over a thousand years. Bacteria get that many rolls of the evolutionary dice between breakfast one day and breakfast the next.

blocks.title: How resistance evolves
items: A huge bacterial population has random variation from mutations.
An antibiotic kills the susceptible cells.
A rare cell with a protective mutation survives.
With competitors gone, it multiplies and takes over.
Repeat with higher doses or new drugs, and resistance stacks up step by step.

blocks.text: The antibiotic did not cause the useful mutation. It removed everything that did not have one. That is the key idea, and it is why the MEGA-plate looks the way it does. Each wall of drug is a filter. Only the rare mutant passes, and then it has an entire empty band to itself.

What do the winning mutations actually do? There are only a few basic strategies, and bacteria use all of them. Some make enzymes that chop the antibiotic apart before it can act, the way staph learned to destroy penicillin. Some change the shape of the molecule the drug is supposed to latch onto, so it no longer fits, like changing the lock so the old key fails. Some build pumps in their outer wall that throw the drug back out as fast as it comes in. And some simply make their walls harder to get through.

items: Destroy it: enzymes that break the antibiotic apart.
Dodge it: change the target so the drug cannot bind.
Eject it: pumps that push the drug out of the cell.
Block it: tighter walls that keep the drug from getting in.

blocks.text: Bacteria have a second weapon that makes this far worse: they share. Many resistance genes sit on small loops of DNA called plasmids that bacteria can pass to each other, sometimes across different species. Imagine if a soldier in one unit could hand their body armor to a soldier in a completely different army just by standing next to them. A resistance gene that evolves in a harmless gut bacterium can end up in a dangerous one.

Resistance usually comes with a price. On the MEGA-plate, the early resistant mutants grew more slowly than their ancestors, because the changes that protected them also got in the way of normal life. Later mutations often fixed that, and the fully resistant strains grew at normal speed again. That second step is bad news. It means that simply stopping use of a drug does not always make resistance disappear, because the bacteria have already paid off the cost.
Antibiotics do not create resistance. They select for it. Every dose is a filter that clears out the vulnerable bacteria and leaves the field to whatever survives.
The warning was there from day one

Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mold contaminating one of his culture plates had killed the bacteria around it. That mold made penicillin. It took until the 1940s, and a massive wartime production effort, to turn it into a drug. When Fleming accepted the Nobel Prize in December 1945, he used part of his lecture to issue a warning that reads today like a prophecy.

He told a story about a hypothetical Mr. X with a sore throat who buys penicillin and takes too little, not enough to kill the bacteria but enough to train them. The surviving resistant germs pass to his wife, who later develops pneumonia. Penicillin fails her, and she dies. Fleming's point was that underdosing was more dangerous than overdosing, because it bred resistance. He was right, and the pattern he predicted has repeated with nearly every antibiotic since.

blocks.title: The race between drugs and bugs
items: Fleming notices mold killing bacteria on a culture plate
Penicillin is mass-produced and saves wartime lives
Fleming's Nobel lecture warns about breeding resistance
Methicillin is introduced to beat penicillin-resistant staph
Methicillin-resistant staph (MRSA) is reported in Britain
MEGA-plate films resistance evolving in about ten days
Global study forecasts more than 39 million resistance deaths by 2050

blocks.text: The story of MRSA shows the speed. By the 1950s, much of the staph bacteria in hospitals had become resistant to penicillin. Chemists responded with methicillin, designed to resist the enzyme staph used to break penicillin down. It came into use in Britain around 1959. Within about two years, doctors were reporting methicillin-resistant staph. Today MRSA is one of the best-known hospital superbugs in the world.
How big the problem really is

The most complete estimate comes from a global research effort called GRAM, which published its latest analysis in The Lancet in 2024. It estimated that in 2021, about 1.14 million deaths worldwide were directly caused by drug-resistant bacterial infections, and resistant bacteria were involved in about 4.7 million deaths in total. Those are infections that once would have been cured with a standard pill.

blocks.title: Deaths directly caused by antibiotic-resistant bacteria, worldwide
blocks.note: The forecast assumes current trends continue; it adds up to more than 39 million deaths from 2025 to 2050.
blocks.source: GRAM study, The Lancet, 2024 (via IHME)

blocks.text: The averages hide a striking split. Between 1990 and 2021, resistance deaths among children under five fell by about 60 percent, thanks to vaccines, cleaner water and better care for infants. But among adults 70 and older they rose by about 90 percent. Older people are more likely to be in hospitals, get surgery and have weaker immune systems, which is exactly where resistant bacteria thrive. As the world's population ages, the forecast rises with it.

items.label: Change in resistance deaths among children under five, 1990 to 2021
Change among adults aged 70 and older over the same period
Deaths directly caused by MRSA in 2021, more than double 1990

blocks.source: GRAM study, The Lancet, 2024 (via IHME)

blocks.text: In the United States, the CDC's most recent full threat report estimated more than 2.8 million antibiotic-resistant infections and 35,000 deaths each year. That was nearly twice the death toll the agency had estimated in its previous report. There was good news inside it, too: deaths had fallen since 2013, and by nearly 30 percent in hospitals, largely because of better infection control.
Why we are not just inventing new drugs

The obvious answer to resistance is to stay ahead with new antibiotics. The problem is economic as much as scientific. A new antibiotic that works against superbugs should be used as little as possible, saved for patients with no other options, so that resistance to it develops slowly. That is great public health and terrible business. A cancer drug or a cholesterol pill that people take every day for years earns back its development costs. A last-resort antibiotic sitting in a hospital cabinet does not, and several companies that brought new antibiotics to market went bankrupt.

The World Health Organization's 2024 review of the pipeline found that the number of antibacterial drugs in clinical testing had risen from 80 to 97. But of 32 antibiotics being developed against the most worrying bacteria, only 12 counted as truly innovative, and only 4 of those worked against at least one of the most critical threats. Since mid-2017, 13 new antibiotics had been approved, and only 2 were from a genuinely new chemical class. Most new drugs are variations on old ones, which bacteria have already practiced beating.

blocks.title: New antibiotics approved since July 2017
blocks.source: World Health Organization, antibacterial pipeline report, 2024

blocks.text: Hospitals are not the only place where the selection happens. A large share of the world's antibiotics goes into farm animals, in some places routinely, to prevent disease in crowded conditions or to speed up growth. Resistant bacteria and their genes can then move from farms into soil, water and food. Many countries have tightened rules on using antibiotics just to fatten livestock, but enforcement varies widely.

Researchers are exploring other routes: viruses called phages that infect bacteria, antibodies, drugs that disarm bacteria instead of killing them, and AI-assisted searches through millions of molecules. Some of these are promising. None is ready to replace antibiotics at scale.
What actually helps

If resistance is natural selection, then fighting it means changing the selection pressure. Use antibiotics less often, and only when they are needed, so fewer resistant strains get a head start. Stop infections from happening and spreading in the first place, so fewer bacteria get the chance to evolve and share genes. The biggest gains so far have come from exactly that: hand hygiene, vaccines, clean water and hospital infection control.

items: Antibiotics do nothing against viruses, which cause most colds, flu and many sore throats. Pushing for them only feeds resistance.
When you are prescribed an antibiotic, take it exactly as directed and ask the corpsman or doctor before stopping early or saving pills.
Never take someone else's leftover antibiotics or share yours.
In a confined space like a ship or submarine, hand washing and not working sick protect the whole crew, not just you.

blocks.text: One note on stopping early: the old rule of always finishing the course is being re-examined, because for some infections shorter courses work just as well and expose bacteria to less drug overall. That is a decision for whoever prescribed it, not something to guess at. The constant is to follow medical advice rather than improvising.
The bigger lesson

The MEGA-plate is worth remembering because it shows something true far beyond bacteria. Whenever you apply strong pressure to a large, fast-changing system, you select for whatever survives the pressure, not for what you intended. Pest control breeds resistant insects. Anti-cheat systems in games breed smarter cheats. Strict metrics at work breed people who game the metric.

The bacteria are not clever. They are numerous, fast and endlessly varied, and that is enough to beat some of the best chemistry humans have ever produced. The only durable strategy against a system like that is to stop handing it easy wins: use the pressure sparingly, and keep the population small.
Evolution needs three things: variation, selection and time. Bacteria have the first in enormous supply and the third in minutes. Every unnecessary antibiotic adds the second.

takeaways: Resistance is natural selection: antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria and leave rare resistant mutants to take over.
On the MEGA-plate, E. coli evolved to survive 1,000 times a lethal dose of trimethoprim in about ten days.
Resistant bacteria directly caused about 1.14 million deaths in 2021, and deaths among people over 70 rose by about 90% since 1990.
New antibiotics are scarce partly because good stewardship means using them as little as possible, which makes them unprofitable.
Antibiotics do nothing for viruses; take them exactly as prescribed and never share or save them.

title: The Yogurt Bacteria That Taught Us to Edit Life
dek: CRISPR started as a germ's immune system against viruses. Now it is curing sickle cell disease, and a baby in Philadelphia got a gene fix built just for him.

blocks.text: In the summer of 2019, a woman from Mississippi named Victoria Gray checked into a hospital in Nashville. She had sickle cell disease, and for most of her life it had meant sudden pain crises severe enough to put her in the emergency room again and again. Doctors took stem cells out of her bone marrow, shipped them to a lab, edited one spot in their DNA, and put them back. Within months her body was making healthy-looking blood. The pain crises stopped.

The tool that did that edit did not come from a medical lab. It came from bacteria, and specifically from scientists who were trying to make better cultures for yogurt and cheese. That is one of the strangest and best stories in modern science: the most powerful genetic tool humans have ever built was stolen, nearly whole, from a microbe's defense against viruses.
This article covers how it works, what it has already done, where the limits are, and why the most important part of the story might be the speed at which it is now moving.
A germ that remembers its enemies

Bacteria have a problem: viruses called phages hunt them constantly. A phage lands on a bacterium, injects its own DNA, and turns the cell into a factory for more phages until it bursts. Bacteria that cannot fight back die. Over billions of years, many of them evolved a defense that works a lot like a wanted poster.

When a bacterium survives a phage attack, it snips out a short chunk of the virus's DNA and pastes it into a special region of its own genome. That region is a stack of these stolen chunks, each separated by the same short repeated sequence. Japanese researchers first noticed the odd repeats in *E. coli* in 1987 without knowing what they were for. Years later they got a clunky name: clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats. CRISPR.

The bacterium copies those stored chunks into short strands of RNA. Each RNA strand pairs up with a protein, and the pair patrols the cell. If the RNA finds viral DNA that matches its sequence, the protein cuts it. The virus is chopped up before it can take over. The cell has a memory of every enemy its ancestors survived, written right into its genes and passed down to its offspring.

The proof that this really was an immune system came in 2007 from a team at Danisco, a food company. They were studying *Streptococcus thermophilus*, a workhorse of the dairy industry, because phage outbreaks can ruin a whole batch of yogurt. They showed that adding a phage's sequence to the CRISPR region made the bacteria resistant to that phage, and removing it took the resistance away. Industrial food science had just found a programmable weapon.

blocks.title: From odd repeats to medicine
items: Japanese researchers spot strange repeated DNA in E. coli
Several labs notice the spacers match viral DNA
Danisco team proves CRISPR is a bacterial immune system
Charpentier and Doudna turn Cas9 into programmable scissors
Labs edit human cells with CRISPR
Nobel Prize in Chemistry to Charpentier and Doudna
Dec 2023
FDA approves Casgevy for sickle cell disease
Feb 2025
Baby KJ gets the first custom-built base editor

blocks.text: Turning a weapon into a tool

The leap came in 2012. Emmanuelle Charpentier, who studied the bacterium that causes strep throat, and Jennifer Doudna, a structural biologist at Berkeley, worked out exactly how one of these cutting proteins, called Cas9, finds its target. Then they did something clever. They showed that you could design the guide RNA yourself, swap in any sequence you wanted, and Cas9 would cut DNA at that spot. Not viral DNA. Any DNA.

That is the whole trick, and it is why CRISPR spread through biology labs like a wildfire. Before it, editing a gene meant engineering a custom protein for every new target, which could take months and a lot of money. With CRISPR, the protein stays the same. You just type a new 20-letter address into the guide RNA. Changing the target became closer to editing a line of code than building a new machine. In 2020 Charpentier and Doudna shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it, an unusually fast award for work only eight years old.

blocks.title: How Cas9 makes a cut
items: Scientists write a guide RNA whose 20 letters match the target spot in the genome.
The guide loads into the Cas9 protein, and the pair drifts through the cell's DNA.
Cas9 grabs onto a short tag sequence next to possible targets and pries the DNA open.
If the guide's letters match the DNA, Cas9 cuts both strands of the double helix.
The cell rushes to repair the break, and that repair is where the edit actually happens.

blocks.text: That last step matters more than most explanations admit. Cas9 does not really edit anything. It breaks the DNA, and the cell fixes the break. The cell's fast repair crew often glues the ends back together sloppily, adding or deleting a few letters. That usually wrecks the gene, which is exactly what you want if your goal is to switch a gene off. If you want a precise change instead, you can supply a template with the correct sequence, and the cell may copy it in. That second route is far less reliable.
The mental model: Cas9 is a search engine attached to a pair of scissors. The guide RNA is the search query. The cut is easy. Controlling what the cell does after the cut is the hard part.
The first cure: switching a baby gene back on

Sickle cell disease comes from a single wrong letter in the gene for adult hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells. That one error makes hemoglobin clump together, bending the cells into rigid crescents that jam in small blood vessels. The result is pain, organ damage and a shorter life. It is one of the most common inherited diseases in the world and falls hardest on people of African descent.

Here is the clever part of the treatment that eventually helped Victoria Gray. It does not fix the broken gene at all. Before birth, everyone makes a different version of hemoglobin, called fetal hemoglobin, which works fine. Around the time of birth, a gene called BCL11A acts like a switch that shuts fetal hemoglobin production down and turns the adult version on. Doctors had long noticed that people who naturally keep making some fetal hemoglobin into adulthood have milder sickle cell disease.

So the therapy, called exa-cel and sold as Casgevy, uses Cas9 to break the BCL11A switch in a patient's blood stem cells. With the switch broken, the cells go back to making fetal hemoglobin, which dilutes the faulty adult kind and keeps red cells round. It is a cut that disables, the easiest thing CRISPR does, aimed at exactly the right target.

items.label: Sickle cell trial participants who went a full year without pain crises
Date the FDA approved Casgevy, the first CRISPR medicine in the US
Estimated cost per patient at approval

blocks.source: Scientific American, reporting FDA approval and trial data, 2023

blocks.text: The results were striking. In the trial data reported at approval, 29 of 30 sickle cell participants went a full year without a pain crisis. Britain's regulator approved the treatment in November 2023, and the US Food and Drug Administration followed on December 8, 2023. It was the first time a CRISPR-based medicine was approved anywhere.

But the honest picture includes the costs. The patient's own stem cells have to be harvested and edited in a specialized lab. Then the patient gets high-dose chemotherapy to wipe out the old bone marrow and make room for the edited cells, which carries real risks including infertility. Recovery means weeks in the hospital. And the price was estimated at up to two million dollars per patient. For a disease that affects millions of people, many in countries with limited health care, that is a cure most patients cannot reach yet.
Beyond scissors: pencils and erasers

Because cutting both strands of DNA is crude, scientists kept building better attachments. The most important upgrade is called base editing, developed in David Liu's lab starting in 2016. A base editor uses a disabled Cas9 that can still find its target but can no longer cut through both strands. Bolted onto it is an enzyme that chemically converts one DNA letter into another. No double-strand break, no messy repair. Just a single letter rewritten in place.

blocks.title: Two ways to change a gene

left.head: Classic Cas9
items: Cuts both strands of DNA
Cell repairs the break, often messily
Great for switching genes off
Precise fixes are unreliable

right.head: Base editing
items: Nicks or does not cut the DNA
Chemically swaps one letter for another
Built for fixing single-letter typos
Fewer large, unwanted changes

blocks.text: That is exactly what a baby in Philadelphia known as KJ needed. He was born in 2024 with severe CPS1 deficiency, a rare disorder in which the liver cannot clear ammonia, a toxic byproduct of breaking down protein. Ammonia builds up in the blood and damages the brain. Many babies with the severe form die young, and the usual long-term answer is a liver transplant.

KJ's mutation was unique to him. So a team at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and Penn Medicine did something nobody had done before: they designed a base editor for his specific typo, packaged it in tiny fat bubbles called lipid nanoparticles that travel to the liver, and had it manufactured in about six months. He got his first dose in late February 2025, with two more in the following months. By the time the results were published in the New England Journal of Medicine that May, he was tolerating more protein in his diet, needed less medication, and had shrugged off a cold without a dangerous ammonia spike. The team was careful to say he needs long-term follow-up.

Look at what changed between those two stories. Casgevy took years to develop and is a single product for a common disease. KJ's treatment was a one-off, built for one child, in months. If that process can be made routine, it flips the economics of rare disease, where thousands of conditions each affect too few people for any company to build a drug the normal way.
The lines we have not crossed (and one person who did)

Every treatment described so far edits *somatic* cells, the ordinary cells of one person's body. Those edits die with the patient. Editing embryos, eggs or sperm is different: those changes would be inherited by every descendant. In 2018 the Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced he had edited embryos that became twin girls, aiming to make them resistant to HIV. The scientific world reacted with near-total condemnation. The edits were medically unnecessary, poorly controlled and done with flawed consent. He was sentenced to prison in China.

There are also technical limits worth knowing. CRISPR can hit the wrong spot when an off-target sequence looks similar enough to the guide. Getting the editor into the right cells is often harder than the edit itself; blood and liver are popular targets precisely because they are the easiest to reach. And many diseases are not caused by one bad gene but by hundreds of small variants interacting with environment. There is no single typo to fix for most heart disease, depression or obesity.

items: Easiest targets: diseases caused by one gene, in tissues you can reach (blood, liver, eye).
Hard targets: brain, muscle throughout the body, and diseases driven by many genes.
Off the table for now: heritable edits to embryos, which scientific bodies broadly oppose.

blocks.text: Why this story is really about debugging

If you have ever written code, CRISPR's history looks familiar. First you need to be able to read the source; that was the Human Genome Project, finished in 2003. Then you need a way to make targeted changes; that was Cas9 in 2012. Then you build better tools for smaller, safer edits, the way programmers moved from rewriting whole files to changing a single line. Medicine is moving from treating symptoms toward patching the source.

The other lesson is about where breakthroughs come from. Nobody set out to find a gene editor in yogurt bacteria. The people who found it were curious about weird repeated DNA and about why dairy cultures kept dying. That kind of basic research looks useless right up until it changes everything. It is a good argument for paying attention to the odd thing you do not understand yet, whether that is a strange pattern in a reactor log or a bug that only happens on Tuesdays.
The pattern to remember: nature already solved a lot of hard engineering problems. Some of the biggest breakthroughs come from noticing a working system and asking what else it could be pointed at.

takeaways: CRISPR is a bacterial immune system: a guide RNA finds a matching DNA sequence and a Cas protein cuts it.
Cas9 only breaks DNA; the cell's own repair process makes the actual change, which is why switching genes off is easier than precise fixes.
The first approved CRISPR cure, Casgevy, works by breaking a switch so sickle cell patients make fetal hemoglobin again.
Base editing rewrites single letters without a full cut, and in 2025 it was custom-built for one baby in about six months.
The biggest limits now are delivery, cost and diseases with no single gene to fix, not the cutting itself.

title: Sending Your Cells the Recipe
dek: mRNA vaccines looked like an overnight miracle in 2020. They were actually thirty years of failure, one stubborn scientist and a fix to a single chemical letter. Now the same trick is being aimed at cancer.

blocks.text: On March 16, 2020, a volunteer in Seattle rolled up a sleeve for an experimental vaccine against a virus the world had first heard of less than three months earlier. Most vaccines take a decade or more to reach that point. This one had gone from a genetic sequence posted online to a needle in an arm faster than it takes to get through some Navy schools.

Nine months later, two vaccines built on the same technology were being given to the public, and their trials showed about 95 percent protection against symptomatic disease. To many people it looked rushed, even suspicious. How do you build a working vaccine in months when it normally takes years?

The real answer is that you don't. The speed in 2020 was the payoff of three decades of slow, unglamorous work, much of it by researchers who could barely get funding. Understanding that story explains both why mRNA vaccines work and why the same platform is now being pointed at cancer.
The messenger in every cell

Your DNA is the master blueprint, and it stays locked in the nucleus of each cell like the original drawings kept in a vault. When a cell needs to build a protein, it makes a temporary working copy of one gene. That copy is messenger RNA, or mRNA. It travels out of the nucleus to a ribosome, the cell's assembly machine, which reads the mRNA three letters at a time and strings together the matching amino acids into a protein.

Then the mRNA is destroyed. Cells chew it up within hours to days, on purpose. That short lifespan is how a cell controls production: stop making the message and the protein stops being built. Think of it as a work order that self-destructs after use rather than a permanent change to the plans.

The idea behind an mRNA vaccine follows directly. Instead of injecting a weakened virus or a purified piece of one, you inject the work order for one viral protein. Your own cells read it, build that protein, and display it. Your immune system sees a protein that does not belong, learns to recognize it, and stays ready for the real virus.

blocks.title: What happens after the shot
items: mRNA for the virus's spike protein is wrapped in tiny fat bubbles called lipid nanoparticles.
The bubbles fuse with cells near the injection site and release the mRNA inside.
Ribosomes read the message and build copies of the spike protein.
Immune cells spot the foreign protein and make antibodies and trained T cells against it.
The mRNA breaks down within days; the immune memory stays.

blocks.text: One common fear is that this changes your DNA. It doesn't. The mRNA never enters the nucleus where DNA is kept, and human cells have no normal way to write RNA back into their own genome. The message is read in the outer part of the cell, used and destroyed, which is exactly what your cells do with their own mRNA all day long.

The elegance of the approach is that the body does the manufacturing. A traditional protein vaccine needs a factory to grow and purify the protein. An mRNA vaccine ships the instructions and lets millions of your own cells act as temporary factories, which is part of why it can be designed and produced so quickly.
Thirty years of the immune system saying no

Scientists knew the basic idea could work by 1990, when a team injected mRNA into mouse muscle and the muscle made the protein it coded for. So why did it take so long? Because the body hated it. Lab-made mRNA set off alarms in the immune system, triggering inflammation and getting destroyed before it could do much. Animals got sick, and protein production was weak.

Katalin Karikó, a Hungarian-born biochemist at the University of Pennsylvania, spent years trying to make mRNA useful as medicine while grant after grant was rejected. She was demoted and pushed toward the edges of academia. Her break came from a chance meeting at a photocopier with Drew Weissman, an immunologist who wanted to build vaccines. Together they asked a precise question: why does our own mRNA not set off the alarm while lab-made mRNA does?

The answer was chemistry. RNA is written in four letters, A, U, G and C, but mammalian cells routinely attach small chemical tweaks to some of those letters. Lab-made mRNA had none. The immune system treated unmodified RNA as a sign of invasion, since that is what viral RNA often looks like. In 2005 Karikó and Weissman showed that swapping in modified versions of one letter, uridine, nearly abolished the inflammatory reaction. Later work showed the modified mRNA also made far more protein.
The key fix was tiny: change one of the four letters slightly so the cell's alarm system reads the message as friendly. That single tweak turned a promising idea into a workable platform.

The other missing piece was packaging. Naked mRNA is fragile and cannot easily get into cells. Researchers working on gene-silencing drugs spent years developing lipid nanoparticles, microscopic fat spheres that protect the cargo and slip it inside cells. By the late 2010s, companies like Moderna and BioNTech had both pieces and were testing mRNA vaccines against flu, Zika and cancer. None had reached the market. Then 2020 happened.

blocks.text: Why it was so fast, and what the trials showed

There was a price for using such a fragile molecule. mRNA falls apart easily, and the first Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine had to be shipped and stored at ultra-cold temperatures, far below an ordinary freezer, which meant special freezers, dry ice and careful logistics. That is one reason the technology was harder to roll out in places without reliable cold chains, and why later work has focused on more stable formulas.

With a traditional vaccine, every new virus means a new manufacturing process: growing the virus in eggs or cells, inactivating it, purifying proteins. With mRNA, the factory stays the same. Only the sequence changes. Once Chinese scientists published the virus's genetic code in January 2020, researchers could design the vaccine on a computer, mostly by picking the right protein to encode. It is closer to swapping one file in a working program than building a new machine.

The fast part was design and the first trials. The slower part, large trials to prove the vaccine works and is safe, still had to happen, and it did, with tens of thousands of volunteers. The trick was running steps in parallel that normally run in sequence, with governments paying to manufacture doses before anyone knew if they would work.

blocks.title: Symptomatic COVID-19 cases in the two big mRNA trials
blocks.note: Pfizer trial had about 43,400 volunteers; Moderna about 30,400. Efficacy was 95% and 94.1%.
blocks.source: Polack et al., NEJM, 2020; Baden et al., NEJM, 2021

blocks.text: The Pfizer-BioNTech trial enrolled about 43,000 people split evenly between vaccine and placebo. Of the 170 people who caught symptomatic COVID-19 during the study window, 162 had gotten the placebo and 8 the vaccine, an efficacy of 95 percent. Moderna's trial of about 30,000 people found 185 cases on placebo against 11 on vaccine, or 94.1 percent. In Moderna's trial, all 30 severe cases were in the placebo group.

Those numbers deserve honest context. They measured protection against symptomatic illness from the original strain, a few months after vaccination. Protection against infection faded over the following months and dropped further as the virus evolved, which is why boosters and updated versions followed. Protection against severe illness held up better. Side effects were real but mostly short: sore arms, fatigue, fever for a day or two. A rare one matters for readers in their twenties: heart inflammation called myocarditis, seen most often in young men after the second dose and usually mild. If you have questions about your own shots, the corpsman or medical officer is the right person to ask.
The next target: your own tumor

Before COVID, cancer was the main thing mRNA companies were working on, and it is where they have returned. The logic is elegant. Cancer cells carry mutations, and some of those mutations produce slightly abnormal proteins called neoantigens that exist nowhere else in your body. If the immune system could be trained to recognize them, it could hunt down cancer cells while ignoring healthy ones.

The problem is that every patient's tumor has a different set of mutations. So the vaccine has to be custom. Doctors sequence a patient's tumor and their normal cells, software picks out the mutations most likely to provoke an immune response, and an mRNA vaccine encoding them is manufactured for that one person. This only makes sense with a platform where changing the sequence is easy. mRNA is that platform.

blocks.title: Melanoma patients free of recurrence at 18 months
blocks.note: 157 patients with high-risk melanoma removed by surgery; a phase 2 trial.
blocks.source: Weber et al., KEYNOTE-942, AACR 2023

blocks.text: The most advanced example is a personalized vaccine from Moderna and Merck. In a phase 2 trial of 157 people whose high-risk melanoma had been surgically removed, patients got either the immunotherapy drug Keytruda alone or Keytruda plus a custom mRNA vaccine encoding up to 34 of their own tumor's neoantigens. After 18 months, 78.6 percent of the combination group were free of recurrence, against 62.2 percent with Keytruda alone, a 44 percent lower risk of the cancer returning or death.

That is promising, not proven. A phase 2 trial is small, and many cancer treatments that shine at this stage disappoint in larger trials. A bigger phase 3 study was launched to test the result properly. Researchers are also testing personalized mRNA vaccines against pancreatic cancer and other tumors, and mRNA versions of flu vaccines, where the ability to update the sequence quickly every season could be a real advantage.

The platform also has limits worth stating plainly. A shot in the arm trains immunity in the blood well but does a weaker job guarding the nose and throat, where respiratory viruses first get in, which is part of why vaccinated people could still catch and spread COVID-19. Side effects like fever are more common than with some older vaccines. And mRNA is not magic for every disease: if scientists do not know which protein to target, a faster factory does not help. Newer variants of the idea, such as self-amplifying RNA that copies itself inside the cell so a smaller dose goes further, are already in use in Japan, which approved one in late 2023.

There is also a political dimension now. The speed of 2020 left some people distrustful, and public funding for mRNA research has swung with that mood. Whatever your view, the science question and the policy question are different. The trial data above are public, large and published, and they are the place to start rather than anyone's headline.
What this story is really about

When Karikó and Weissman won the Nobel Prize in 2023, the committee pointed specifically to their 2005 finding about modified letters, published fifteen years before the pandemic. For most of those fifteen years, almost nobody cared. The paper did not make headlines. The work only looked obvious in hindsight, after it saved enormous numbers of lives.

There is a lesson there about how progress actually happens. The visible breakthrough in 2020 sat on top of decades of work that looked like failure from the outside: rejected grants, a demotion, mice that got sick, a packaging problem nobody had solved. Platforms take a long time to build and then suddenly pay off all at once, because every new use reuses the same foundation.

That pattern shows up far outside biology. A game engine, a content channel, a skill like reading reactor plant drawings: the first year looks slow and unrewarding. Then one day the foundation is in place and new things come together fast. From outside, it looks like overnight success. From inside, it was years of fixing one letter at a time.
Platforms are slow to build and fast to use. The question to ask about any long project is not how much it has produced yet, but whether it is turning into something you can reuse.

takeaways: mRNA is a temporary work order: cells read it, build a protein and destroy it within days. It never enters the nucleus or changes DNA.
The breakthrough that made it work was a small chemical change to one RNA letter, published in 2005 and largely ignored for years.
The 2020 vaccines were fast because the platform already existed; only the sequence had to change.
Trials showed about 95% protection against symptomatic COVID-19 at first, which faded against infection over time but held better against severe illness.
Personalized mRNA cancer vaccines showed a promising result in melanoma, but larger trials still have to confirm it.

title: The Brain That Grew a Map of London
dek: Learning is not just storing information. It physically rebuilds the organ doing the learning, and the same process that makes you skilled can also lock in the habits you wish you did not have.

blocks.text: To drive a black cab in London, you have to pass a test called the Knowledge. It requires memorizing roughly 25,000 streets within six miles of Charing Cross station, plus thousands of landmarks, and being able to recite the best route between any two points on demand, out loud, to an examiner. Trainees ride around the city on scooters for years. It typically takes three to four years, and many never make it.

Neuroscientists Katherine Woollett and Eleanor Maguire saw an experiment hiding in that ordeal. They recruited 79 trainee cabbies at the start of their training, plus 31 people who were not training, and scanned all of their brains. Years later they scanned them again. Only 39 of the trainees had qualified and came back for the second scan, and 20 more who had failed also returned.

In the trainees who passed, a specific part of the brain, the back of the hippocampus, had gained gray matter. In those who failed, and in the controls, it had not changed. Before training, all three groups had looked the same. The difference appeared only after years of hard spatial learning, and only in the people who did the learning successfully. Memorizing a city had physically reshaped their brains.

The design matters. Years earlier, Maguire's group had found that experienced London cabbies had larger posterior hippocampi than other people, and that the effect grew with years on the job. But that kind of snapshot cannot rule out the reverse explanation: maybe people born with a bigger hippocampus are drawn to the job and better at passing the test. Scanning the same people before and after, and comparing those who passed with those who failed, is what made the case that the learning caused the change.

items.label: London streets trainee cabbies must learn
Trainees scanned at the start vs those who qualified and were rescanned
Typical time to pass the Knowledge

blocks.text: What actually changes when you learn

Your brain has tens of billions of neurons, each connected to thousands of others through junctions called synapses. A thought, a memory or a skill is not stored in one cell. It lives in a pattern of connections, a particular set of neurons that tend to fire together. Learning means changing that pattern, and the brain can change it in several physical ways.

The most basic is strengthening synapses. In 1949 the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed that when one neuron repeatedly helps make another fire, the link between them gets stronger. It is often summarized as cells that fire together wire together. In 1973 researchers found the cellular version of this in the hippocampus of rabbits: a burst of activity made a synapse respond more strongly for hours afterward. It is called long-term potentiation, and it is still one of the main models of how memories form.

blocks.title: How practice rewires a circuit
items: You attempt a skill, and a specific chain of neurons fires together.
Repeated firing strengthens the synapses along that chain, so the signal passes more easily.
Neurons grow new connection points and prune ones that go unused.
Heavily used pathways get extra insulation called myelin, which speeds up signals.
Over time the skill runs with less effort and less conscious attention.

blocks.text: Beyond stronger synapses, neurons can sprout new connection points and lose old ones. Support cells wrap well-used nerve fibers in more myelin, a fatty insulation that makes signals travel faster and more reliably, a bit like upgrading from bare wire to shielded cable. Blood supply to busy regions can increase. Add all of that up across millions of cells, and the change can become large enough to show up on an MRI scan as more gray matter.

Losing connections is as important as gaining them. A young child's brain makes far more synapses than it will keep, and through childhood and the teenage years it prunes the ones that go unused, the way a sculptor removes stone. Expertise often looks less like adding more wiring everywhere and more like a cleaner, more efficient circuit with the useless branches cut away.
Practice does not just make a skill feel easier. It builds faster, better-insulated wiring for that skill. That is why something that once took all your concentration eventually runs on autopilot.
Use it, or the brain takes it back

The London cabbies are an extreme case, but smaller versions show up wherever scientists look. In 1995, a team scanned the brains of violin, cello and guitar players. The area of the touch-sensing cortex devoted to the fingers of the left hand, the hand that presses the strings, was larger than in non-musicians. The right hand, which bows or strums, showed no such difference. And the earlier a musician had started playing, the bigger the change.

In 2004, German researchers taught a small group of young adults to juggle three balls. Brain scans after they had mastered it showed growth in gray matter in regions that track moving objects. Then the jugglers stopped practicing for three months. On the next scan, the gain had shrunk, and many of them could no longer do the routine. The brain had built the hardware when it was needed and started dismantling it when it was not.

This is the part of neuroplasticity that is easy to miss. The brain is not a hard drive filling up with files. It is more like a city that keeps reallocating land. Brain tissue is expensive to run, burning a large share of your body's energy, and it does not keep unused circuits at full strength forever. Skills you practice get more space. Skills you abandon slowly lose it.

The taxi study found a trade-off too. Qualified cabbies were better than controls at judging distances between London landmarks, but worse at recalling a complex drawing after a 30-minute delay. The researchers were careful about what this means, and it is one result, not a law. But it hints that brain resources are not unlimited, and getting much better at one kind of thing may come with costs somewhere else.
Windows that close, and ones that do not

In the 1960s, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel ran experiments that won them a Nobel Prize and showed the darker side of plasticity. They found that if a kitten had one eye kept closed during a critical window early in life, the visual part of its brain rewired to favor the open eye. Open the closed eye later, and it never fully recovered, even though the eye itself was healthy. The same closure in an adult cat had little lasting effect.

Human brains also have critical periods, windows when certain circuits are especially easy to shape. It is why children who learn a language young usually speak it without an accent, while adults rarely manage that. For a long time, scientists took this to mean the adult brain was basically fixed, a finished building with no more construction allowed.

That view was wrong. The taxi drivers were adults. So were the jugglers. Adult brains are less plastic than children's in some ways, but they keep changing for life. The difference is that adult change seems to depend more on attention, effort and repetition. A child soaks up a language passively; an adult has to work at it. That is less a closed door than a door that now needs a push.

Medicine has put this to work. After a stroke damages the part of the brain controlling one arm, patients naturally lean on the good arm, and the weak one gets weaker. Constraint-induced movement therapy, developed by psychologist Edward Taub, who was also part of the string-player study, flips that. The good arm is restrained for much of the day, forcing hours of practice with the weak one. In many patients, other parts of the brain take over some of the lost control. The brain reorganizes, but only because it is pushed to.
